text: Scene 4 - Meeting Lady Wotton
speaker: C5

text: Lord Henry’s house - somewhere in Mayfair. Dorian was waiting. Lord Henry had not yet come in. He was always late on principle.
speaker: C6

text: His principle being that punctuality is the thief of time
speaker: C5

text: At last he heard a step outside, and the door opened.
speaker: C8

text: It was Lady Wotton. She was a curious woman whose dresses always looked as if they had been designed in a rage and put on in a tempest.
speaker: Lady W

text: She was usually in love with someone and as her passions had never been returned, she had kept all her illusions.
speaker: C4

text: How late you are, Harry!
speaker: Dorian

text: I am afraid it is not Harry, Mr Gray.
speaker: Lady W

text: I beg your pardon I thought …
speaker: Dorian

text: You thought it was my husband. It is only his wife. I know you quite well by your photographs. I think my husband has got seventeen of them.
speaker: Lady W

text: Not seventeen?
speaker: Dorian

text: Well, eighteen, then. And I saw you with him the other night at the opera. I like Wagner's music better than anybody's. It is so loud that one can talk the whole time without other people hearing what one says. That is a great advantage, don't you think so, Mr Gray?
speaker: Lady W

text: I am afraid I don't think so, I never talk during music - at least, during good music. If one hears bad music, it is one's duty to drown it in conversation.
speaker: Dorian

text: Ah! that is one of Harry's views, isn't it, Mr Gray? I always hear Harry's views from his friends. It is the only way I get to know of them. But you must not think I don’t like good music - I adore it but it does make me too romantic. I have worshipped pianists - two at a time sometimes. I don’t know what it is about them - perhaps it’s that they are foreigners. They all are aren’t they. Even those who are born in England become foreigners after a time - it’s so clear of them and a compliment to art. You’ve never been to one of my parties have you? You must come. I can’t afford orchids but I spare no expense in foreigners. They make ones rooms look so picturesque.
speaker: Lady W

text: But here is Harry! Harry, I came in to look for you, to ask you something - I forget what it was - and I found Mr Gray here. He has been most pleasant. I am so glad I've seen him.
speaker: Lady W

text: I am charmed, my love, quite charmed. So sorry I am late, Dorian. I went to look after a piece of old brocade in Wardour Street and had to bargain for hours for it. Nowadays people know the price of everything and the value of nothing.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: I am afraid I must be going I have promised to drive with the Duchess. Good-bye, Mr Gray. Good-bye, Harry. You are dining out, I suppose? So am I. Perhaps I shall see you at Lady Thornbury’s.
speaker: Lady W

text: Never marry. Men marry because they are tired, women, because they are curious. Both are disappointed.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: I don't think I am likely to marry, Harry. I am too much in love.
speaker: Dorian

text: Who are you in love with?
speaker: Lord Henry

text: With an actress.
speaker: Dorian

text: That is a rather commonplace debut.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: You would not say so if you saw her, Harry.
speaker: Dorian

text: Who is she?
speaker: Lord Henry

text: Her name is Sibyl Vane.
speaker: Dorian

text: Never heard of her.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: No one has. People will someday, however. She is a genius.
speaker: Dorian

text: How long have you known her?
speaker: Lord Henry

text: About three weeks.
speaker: Dorian

text: And where did you come across her?
speaker: Lord Henry

text: It never would have happened if I had not met you. You filled me with a wild desire to know everything about life. One evening I determined to go out in search of some adventure. I don't know what I expected, but I went out and wandered eastward, soon losing my way in a labyrinth of grimy streets. I passed by an absurd little theatre, with great flaring gas jets and gaudy play-bills.
speaker: Dorian

text: A hideous man, who appeared to be the manager, was standing at the entrance. He wore the most amazing waistcoat.
speaker: C4

text: He was smoking a vile cigar.
speaker: C5

text: Have a box, my Lord.
speaker: C4

text: He said, when he saw me, and he took off his hat with an air of gorgeous servility. There was something about him, Harry, that amused me. He was such a monster. You will laugh at me, I know, but I really went in and paid a whole guinea for the stage-box. Well, I found myself seated in a horrid little private box, with a vulgar drop scene staring me in the face. I looked out from behind the curtain and surveyed the house.
speaker: Dorian

text: A tawdry affair. The gallery and pit were fairly full,
speaker: C6

text: but the two rows of dingy stalls were quite empty. Women went about with oranges and ginger-beer, and there was a terrible consumption of nuts going on.
speaker: C8

text: The play was Romeo and Juliet. There was a dreadful orchestra, presided over by a young man who sat at a cracked piano.
speaker: C1

text: That nearly drove me away, but at last the drop-scene was drawn up and the play began.
speaker: Dorian

text: Romeo was a stout elderly gentleman, with corked eyebrows, a husky tragedy voice, and a figure like a beer-barrel.
speaker: C4

text: Mercutio was almost as bad. He was played by the low-comedian, who had introduced gags of his own and was on most friendly terms with the pit.
speaker: C8

text: But Juliet! Harry, imagine….
speaker: Dorian

text: A young woman, with an enchanting face, dark hair and eyes that were amber wells of passion, lips that were soft like the petals of a rose.
speaker: Sibyl

text: She was the loveliest thing I had ever seen in my life.
speaker: Dorian

text: And her voice — I’d never heard such a voice. It was very low at first, with deep mellow notes that seemed to fall singly upon one’s ear.
speaker: Dorian

text: Go ask his name: if he be married My grave is like to be my wedding bed.
speaker: Sibyl

text: Then it became a little louder, and sounded like a flute or a distant hautboy.
speaker: Dorian

text: My only love sprung from my only hate! Too early seen unknown, and known too late! Prodigious birth of love it is to me, That I must love a loathed enemy
speaker: Sibyl

text: In the garden-scene it had all the tremulous ecstasy that one hears just before dawn when nightingales are singing.
speaker: Dorian

text: O Romeo, Romeo! Wherefore art thou Romeo? Deny thy father and refuse his name; Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love, And I’ll no longer be a Capulet.
speaker: Sibyl

text: There were moments, later on, when it had the wild passion of violins.
speaker: Dorian

text: O, swear not by the moon, the innocent moon, That monthly changes in her cycled orb, Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.
speaker: Sibyl

text: You know how a voice can stir one. Your voice and the voice of Sibyl Vane are two things that I shall never forget and each of them says something different. Harry, I love her. She is everything to me in life. Night after night I go to see her play. One evening she is Rosalind, and the next evening she is Imogen. I have seen her die, I have watched her disguised as a pretty boy. She has been mad, and she has been innocent. Ordinary women never appeal to one's imagination. But how different an actress is! Harry! why didn't you tell me that the only thing worth loving is an actress?
speaker: Dorian

text: Because I have loved so many of them.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: Oh, yes, horrid people with dyed hair and painted faces.
speaker: Dorian

text: Don’t run down dyed hair and painted faces. There is an extraordinary charm in them, sometimes.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: I wish now I had not told you about Sibyl Vane.
speaker: Dorian

text: You could not have helped telling me, Dorian. All through your life you will tell me everything you do.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: Yes, Harry, I believe that is true. You have a curious influence over me.
speaker: Dorian

text: Now tell me what are your actual relations with Sibyl Vane?
speaker: Lord Henry

text: Harry! She is sacred!
speaker: Dorian

text: It is only the sacred things that are worth touching. But when did you first speak to this actress.
speaker: Lord A

text: The third night. She had been playing Rosalind. I could not help going round. I had thrown her some flowers, and she had looked at me. Oh, she was so shy and so gentle and she seemed quite unconscious of her power. I think we were both rather nervous. The old manager stood grinning at the doorway of the dusty greenroom, while we stood looking at each other like children. He would insist on calling me 'My Lord,' so I had to assure Sibyl that I was not anything of the kind. She said quite simply
speaker: Dorian

text: You look more like a prince. I must call you Prince Charming.
speaker: Sibyl

text: Miss Sibyl knows how to pay compliments.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: You don't understand her, Harry. She knows nothing of life. She lives with her mother, a faded tired woman who played Lady Capulet on the first night, and looks as if she had seen better days.
speaker: Dorian

text: I know that look. It depresses me. You can dine with me to-night, can't you?
speaker: Lord Henry

text: Not tonight. To-night she is Imogen and tomorrow night she will be Juliet.
speaker: Dorian

text: When is she Sibyl Vane?
speaker: Lord Henry

text: Never.
speaker: Dorian

text: I congratulate you.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: I want you and Basil to come with me some night and see her act. I must get her out of the manager’s hands. She is bound to him for three years. I shall have to pay him something, of course. When all that is settled, I shall take a West End theatre and bring her out properly.
speaker: Dorian

text: Well, what night shall we go?
speaker: Lord Henry

text: Let us fix tomorrow. She plays Juliet tomorrow.
speaker: Dorian

text: All right. The Bristol at eight o'clock and I will get Basil.
speaker: Lord Henry

text: Dear Basil! I have not laid eyes on him for a week. It is rather horrid of me, as he has sent me my portrait in the most wonderful frame, specially designed by himself. He is the best of fellows, but he seems to me to be just a bit of a Philistine. Since I have known you, Harry, I have discovered that. And now I am off. Don't forget about to-morrow.
speaker: Dorian

text: Lord Henry watched him go. Certainly few people had ever interested him so much.
speaker: C2

text: He was conscious that it was through certain words of his, that Dorian’s soul had turned to this girl and bowed in worship before her
speaker: C2

text: While Lord Henry sat dreaming on these things, his valet entered and reminded him it was time to dress for dinner.
speaker: C4

text: Later, when he arrived home, he saw a telegram lying on the hall table. He opened it and found it was from Dorian Gray.
speaker: C4

text: It was to tell him that Dorian was engaged to be married.
speaker: C8
